title: Describing Phonetic Variation in Words: Seseo, Ceceo, and Syllable-Final -s

sections.content: When linguists, journalists, and educated speakers discuss Spanish accents, they rely on a concise set of descriptive terms. Because Spanish orthography is largely shared across twenty countries, major pronunciation differences do not change how words are spelled, but they give each regional variety its distinct phonetic profile (*el rasgo fonético*).

The widest phonetic division involves the sounds written *s*, *c* (before *e, i*), and *z*. All of Latin America, the Canary Islands, and much of Andalusia practise *el seseo*: pronouncing *casa* and *caza* with the same /s/ sound. Northern and central Spain maintain a distinction between /s/ (*casa*) and the interdental sound /θ/ (*caza, cine*), while parts of southern Andalusia practise *el ceceo* (using a sound close to /θ/ for both). A second major feature across the Caribbean, coastal Colombia, Chile, the River Plate, and southern Spain is *la aspiración* (softening or dropping of *-s* at the end of a syllable, as in *los mismos*). Among all these patterns, *el seseo* is the majority pronunciation of the Spanish-speaking world and enjoys full normative prestige.

sections.title: Key Terms for Describing Spanish Pronunciation
rows: Pronouncing *c* (before *e/i*), *z*, and *s* alike as /s/ (all of Latin America, Canary Islands, parts of Andalusia — full standard prestige)
Distinguishing /s/ in *casa* from interdental /θ/ in *caza* (northern and central Spain)
Pronouncing both *s* and *z/c* with a sound similar to /θ/ (parts of southern Andalusia)
Softening or omitting *-s* at the end of a *sílaba* before a *consonante* or pause (Caribbean, coasts, Southern Cone, southern Spain)
The melodic contour of speech, which often identifies a speaker's region before any individual word

items.spanish: El seseo es el rasgo fonético mayoritario del español y tiene el mismo valor culto que la distinción peninsular.
items.english: Seseo is the majority phonetic feature of Spanish and has the same educated standing as the peninsular distinction.

items.spanish: Gracias al seseo, palabras como «taza» y «tasa» suenan igual en toda América Latina, aunque mantienen su escritura diferente.
items.english: Thanks to seseo, words like 'taza' (cup) and 'tasa' (rate) sound identical across Latin America, although they keep their distinct spelling.

items.spanish: La aspiración de la consonante final de sílaba es habitual en el Caribe, en las costas del Pacífico y en el Río de la Plata.
items.english: The aspiration of the syllable-final consonant is common in the Caribbean, on the Pacific coasts, and in the River Plate region.

items.spanish: A menudo reconocemos el origen de un hablante por la entonación de la frase antes que por un sonido aislado.
items.english: We often recognize a speaker's origin by the intonation of the sentence sooner than by an isolated sound.

sections.content: Do not confuse *el seseo* with a spelling change: speakers who practise *el seseo* pronounce *caza* and *casa* with the same /s/ sound, yet in writing they distinguish *z*, *c*, and *s* under the exact same spelling rules as every other Spanish speaker.
